headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: AutoGen and Open Interpreter both write/read the same local workspace, while Open Interpreter’s default filesystem reach is broader and less isolated.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and uses stdin/stdout tool calls; Open Interpreter has clipboard and filesystem access, so content from one can be manually or programmatically bridged into the other. The pair lacks a documented provenance barrier, making instruction-hijack via shared files plausible in default setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same working directory or clipboard bridge
IF either agent treats file or pasted content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent in under 5 minutes
Disable clipboard-based transfer between agents
Add a human review step before copying outputs into the other agent
Run Open Interpreter in Docker mode if available
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all inter-agent artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen touches application data and model-provider API keys, while Open Interpreter can reach the entire user filesystem at user privilege. Because both can read/write local files and Open Interpreter’s isolation is none by default, sensitive data can flow from the shared workspace into broader local access or model calls.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared workspace
IF Open Interpreter is allowed to inspect or transmit those files through configured model providers
mitigations: Move secrets out of the shared workspace
Restrict Open Interpreter to a dedicated subdirectory
Enable Docker mode for Open Interpreter
Rotate any exposed API keys
requires-engineering: enforce file allowlists for both agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen and Open Interpreter both have shell, subprocess, filesystem read/write, and broad network egress. Open Interpreter additionally modifies git state and shares state via filesystem, so concurrent writes to the same directory can collide and corrupt work or repository history.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory or git repository
IF they run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories
Serialize write operations with a simple manual lock
Avoid concurrent git edits by Open Interpreter
Snapshot the repo before either agent writes
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool outputs and code, and Open Interpreter can act on local machine state and code blocks. If Open Interpreter consumes AutoGen output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into real actions, especially because Open Interpreter’s default confirmation can be bypassed with auto_run.
conditions: IF AutoGen output is forwarded into Open Interpreter without verification
IF Open Interpreter is started with auto_run or equivalent unattended execution
mitigations: Require a human to verify AutoGen outputs before execution
Keep Open Interpreter confirmation prompts enabled
Use a checklist for any generated commands
Limit AutoGen to drafting only
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen’s docs indicate configurable self-isolation, while Open Interpreter defaults to no isolation and can access the entire user filesystem. That mismatch can create retention and residency exposure for local data handled by both agents, even though both are open-source and no specific HIPAA/GDPR certification gap is stated.
conditions: IF regulated or sensitive data is placed in the shared workspace
IF Open Interpreter runs without Docker or equivalent isolation
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Enable Open Interpreter Docker mode
Document a retention policy for generated artifacts
Purge temporary files after each session
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls
